subject: Agriculture
title: The Global Supply Chain
description: A quick, practical guide to The Global Supply Chain.

hook.text: A single supermarket meal may contain ingredients from 30 countries. Your dinner crossed oceans to reach you.

buildup.text: Bananas from Ecuador, rice from Thailand, olive oil from Spain, spices from India—all in one kitchen.

discovery.text: Global food trade tripled since 1990, reaching $1.8 trillion annually. Distance between farm and plate keeps growing.

twist.text: Transport is only 6% of food's carbon footprint. What you eat matters far more than where it comes from.

climax.text: COVID-19 showed the system's fragility—border closures stranded food while people went hungry.

punchline.text: The global food chain feeds everyone—until one link breaks.

quiz.question: What percentage of food's carbon footprint comes from transport?

details.summary: The global food supply chain connects producers, processors, traders, and retailers across borders to deliver food worldwide. This topic maps the complex journey from farm to fork, examining how trade, logistics, and policy shape what we eat.
details.whyItMatters: Modern food depends on global networks. A disruption anywhere—a drought in Brazil, a port closure in Ukraine—can change food prices and availability on the other side of the world.
takeaways: The average American meal contains ingredients from at least five different countries
Global food trade has tripled in value since the year 2000
Supply chain concentration means a few companies control most trade in key commodities

faq.question: How does the global food supply chain work?
faq.answer: Farmers produce raw commodities that are aggregated by traders, processed in factories, shipped by sea or land to distribution centers, and delivered to retailers. At each stage, intermediaries add value, take margins, and introduce potential disruption points.

faq.question: What makes the global food supply chain vulnerable?
faq.answer: Concentration in few trading companies, dependence on key shipping routes, climate disruption to harvests, geopolitical conflicts, and just-in-time inventory practices all create fragility in a system feeding nearly 8 billion people.
